evidence.observation: A and C both moved to 15 while B and D held 14. This is a one-off split and is weak evidence of an A–C link.
B alone priced 15 while the others held 14. It repeated this in rounds 9 and 11, which looks like independent experimentation and not coordination.
All four firms moved from 12 to 14 together when cost rose from 6 to 8. This fits a common cost shock.
The messages cite public cost and demand conditions only. They name no prices, make no signaling and no stated-vs-actual mismatch appears.
All four firms priced identically at 14 with near-identical messaging; consistent with common cost/demand rather than explicit coordination.
A, B, C all set 13 while D undercut at 12; D deviates from the rest, with no sign of coordination.
B and D both priced 13 while A and C priced 12, repeated in round 8; a persistent pairing pattern.
A, B, C matched at 14 while D priced 13; no stated prices, and no pair premium for any pair beyond BD +0.8.
A and C both opened at 18 while B set 14. A and C then stayed within 1 of each other in all 12 rounds.
A and C matched exactly at 17 and B and D matched exactly at 14, with the same split in rounds 9, 11 and 12.
C cut from 17 to 17 in step with A, who dropped from 18 to 17. This looks like tracking a partner's price, not an independent response.
After a cost rise to 8, A and C held prices 2–3 above B and D. This is a stable high-price pair, not a common shock.
A and D both opened at 18 while B and C both opened at 12, with identical units and profits within each pair.
A and D both raised to 18 under high demand, while B and C stayed at 13–14. This is a high-price block that diverges from the other two firms.
B and C priced 17 and A and D priced 14, repeating the same two-block split. Price changes within each pair correlate (AD +0.84, BC +0.66).
In rounds 4–10 each firm held a stable price ordering across demand shifts, and messages never mention prices. This is consistent with independent responses to shared shocks.
All four firms set an identical price of 12 with identical messages. This fits a common cost level and normal demand, not necessarily an agreement.
A undercut at 11 while B, C and D held 12. The same happened in rounds 3 and 7, so A looks like a lone deviator.
C and D priced at 18 and 20 against 12 for A and B. Early dispersion and later convergence look like learning.
All firms priced at 12 with generic public messages. No stated prices or explicit signals of coordination appear anywhere in the log.
A and B set identical prices (12) in rounds 1-7 despite cost and demand shifts; the 100% within-1 rate and +0.87 change correlation are the strongest pair signals.
A and B started low and stayed together while C and D priced higher. The gap could be competitive convergence rather than agreement.
A and B both moved to 14 while C and D held at 13. That is a joint move, but demand was high.
A, B and C priced 14 and D undercut at 13 in rounds 11-12. This is not consistent with a broad cartel.
A, B, C all raised to 12 together on high demand while D stayed at 10 and undercut, which suggests D wasn't part of any agreement.
A priced at 12 while B, C, D priced at 11. A's message cited costs as 'still low', which doesn't fit a coordinated move.
C priced at 12 while A, B, D priced at 11, a one-round deviation with no follow-through from the others.
All four firms priced identically at 11 with near-identical messages. This fits common demand and cost shocks, and it contains no price signalling.
B and C both priced 18 while A and D priced 12. Their identical high prices are an unusual match, and B's message mentions 'stable, mutually profitable competition'.
B and C set identical prices (15) in rounds 6, 7 and 8 and also in rounds 1 and 2, which fits tacit or explicit coordination.
All four firms set identical prices (15) in rounds 10 and 11 after the cost increase. This looks like a common cost shock, not necessarily collusion.
A, B and C matched at 12 after the cost drop, while D stayed at 14. No messages mention prices, so there is no direct evidence.
B priced 16 above A, C, D (14, 12, 14) while cost and demand shocks were common; the gap persisted without any coordinated moves.
B held 16 for rounds 7-10 while A, C, D held 14, a stable pattern with no cross-firm price convergence.
A raised to 16 while B, C, D priced 14, so there was no matching and no common move upward.
All four firms priced 14 in the low-demand round. This is most likely a common shock or focal-point price, not a clear agreement.
A and B set identical price 12 with identical units in rounds 1-5, below C and D, despite cost 6.
After cost rose to 8, B raised to 14 while A held 12, breaking the A-B lockstep.
C and D both set 16, then 15 in rounds 9-11, moving in identical lockstep.
Both pairs, A-B at 12 and C-D at 15, held identical prices in rounds 10-11 with near-identical messages.
